definition.text: A physical quantity often described as a measure of how spread out, or dispersed, energy is in a system; loosely, its degree of disorder.

facts.text: By the second law of thermodynamics, the entropy of an isolated system tends not to decrease.
Lower entropy marks more useful energy: energy supplied at a high temperature tends to be more useful than the same amount at a lower temperature.
Rudolf Clausius named the concept in 1865, from the Greek word for 'transformation'.
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen brought entropy into ecological economics, coining 'entropy pessimism', a position Herman Daly continued to promote.
Because of rising entropy, recovering materials dispersed as pollution and waste needs energy and resources that rise steeply as the recycled share grows.
Entropy is the only physical quantity that seems to give time a direction, sometimes called the arrow of time.

definition.text: The maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system as it comes into balance with its surroundings; often called 'available energy'.

facts.text: It depends on both the system and its environment, arising from the difference between them.
Energy in and out always balance by the first law, but in real processes part of the exergy input is always destroyed, as the second law requires.
Solar radiation provides most of the exergy for processes on Earth, including those that sustain life.
Exergy use has spread from engineering to industrial ecology, ecological economics and systems ecology.
Some systems ecologists see exergy as the natural world's analogue of economic currency.
Zoran Rant proposed the concept in 1956, extending work by Gibbs and Helmholtz.

definition.text: How much of a form of energy can be turned into useful work, measured as the ratio of its exergy to its energy.

facts.text: Electrical, kinetic and chemical energy are fully recoverable as work, so their exergy equals their energy.
Heat and radiation cannot be fully converted to work; the upper limit for heat is the Carnot efficiency, found by Sadi Carnot in 1824.
High-exergy energy carriers can do more kinds of work and so can be held to have more economic value.

definition.text: Proposals to use exergy analysis to make environmental policy fairer and more effective.

facts.text: Exergy analysis exposed a gap in national greenhouse gas balances, which often leave out emissions from international transport and so ignore import and export impacts.
Early cases suggest exergy-based taxation could reduce the tax burden on citizens.

definition.text: The work potential lost, or wasted, in a real process; also called irreversibility.

facts.text: Highly efficient systems destroy little exergy, and inefficient ones a lot.
The exergy destroyed in a cycle is the sum of that destroyed in each of its processes.
